separable: inseparable — *dabble in photography*, *dabble in it*; never ✗ *dabble photography in*.
gloss: To do something occasionally as a hobby, without taking it seriously.
examples: He *dabbles in* photography on the weekends.
She *dabbled in* local politics for a year and quit.
They have been *dabbling in* real estate since the move.

separable: separable — *dash off a note* / *dash a note off*, and with a pronoun it must split: *dash it off*.
gloss: To write or produce something very quickly and without much care.
examples: Let me *dash off* a quick email before we leave.
She *dashed* the whole report *off* in under an hour.
He has *dashed off* three drafts since breakfast.

separable: no object — nothing can come between the two words; the time follows *to*: *dates back to 1740*.
gloss: To have existed since a particular time in the past.
examples: The church *dates back* to 1740.
Their argument *dated back* thirty years.
We found letters *dating back* to the war.

separable: inseparable — the person follows *on*: *it dawned on me*, never ✗ *it dawned me on*. The subject is almost always *it* plus a *that*-clause.
gloss: To become suddenly clear to someone.
examples: It finally *dawned on* me that she had been joking.
The truth *dawns on* him a little late every time.
It was *dawning on* all of us that the power was not coming back.

separable: separable — *deck out the hall* / *deck the hall out*, and *deck it out*. Most often passive: *decked out in*.
gloss: To decorate something or dress someone in a showy way.
examples: They *deck out* the square with lights every December.
We *decked* the whole porch *out* for Halloween.
The lobby was *decked out* in red and gold.

separable: inseparable — *deliver on a promise*, *deliver on it*; never ✗ *deliver a promise on*.
gloss: To actually do what you promised or were expected to do.
examples: The new manager *delivered on* every promise he made.
Can a team that small *deliver on* a deadline like that?
The company has never *delivered on* its pledge to cut prices.

ru: наводнять, наводнить (о толпе); сваливаться, свалиться (на кого-л.)
separable: inseparable — the place or person follows *on*: *descended on the town*, never ✗ *descended the town on*.
gloss: To arrive somewhere in large numbers, usually without being invited.
examples: Tourists *descend on* the town every July.
Reporters *descended on* the courthouse within the hour.
Relatives have been *descending on* the house all week.

separable: separable — *dial back the rhetoric* / *dial the rhetoric back*, and *dial it back*.
gloss: To reduce something that has gone too far.
examples: Let us *dial back* the sarcasm a little.
They *dialed* the pressure *back* after the first week.
He has *dialed back* his hours since the surgery.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *dialed*, *dialing*. British English doubles it: *dialled*, *dialling*.

separable: separable — *dial down the volume* / *dial the volume down*, and *dial it down*.
gloss: To make something less loud, less bright, or less intense.
examples: Could you *dial down* the drama for one evening?
She *dialed* the lights *down* for the movie.
They are *dialing down* expectations for the quarter.
contrast: *Dial down* and *dial back* overlap. *Dial down* suits a level you can picture on a knob — volume, heat, lights; *dial back* suits behavior, spending, or a plan.

separable: separable — *dial in the settings* / *dial the settings in*, and *dial it in*. Very often passive: *the recipe is dialed in*.
gloss: To adjust something until it is working exactly right.
examples: It took two hours to *dial in* the espresso grind.
He *dialed* the suspension *in* the night before the race.
The lighting is finally *dialed in*.

ru: подключаться, подключиться по телефону (к совещанию); созваниваться, созвониться
separable: no object — nothing sits between the two words; the meeting follows *to*: *dial in to the call*.
gloss: To join a meeting by phone or conference line instead of in person.
examples: Three of us will *dial in* from Denver.
She *dialed in* about five minutes late.
He is *dialing in* from the airport again.

separable: separable — *dial up the pressure* / *dial the pressure up*, and *dial it up*.
gloss: To increase something deliberately.
examples: The coach wants to *dial up* the pressure in the second half.
They *dialed* the marketing *up* before the holidays.
He has *dialed up* the intensity since the trade.

separable: no object — *the noise died away*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To grow fainter and fainter until it can no longer be heard.
examples: The applause slowly *died away*.
Voices *die away* as you walk deeper into the canyon.
The engine noise was *dying away* down the valley.
contrast: Spelling trap: *die* → *dying*, never ✗ *dieing*. The *-ie* becomes *-y* before *-ing*.

separable: no object — *the wind died down*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To become much weaker, quieter, or calmer.
examples: The wind *died down* around midnight.
Wait until the noise *dies down* before you call.
The story has *died down* since the apology.
contrast: Spelling trap: *die* → *dying*, never ✗ *dieing*.

ru: вымирать, вымереть (постепенно); гибнуть, погибнуть (один за другим)
separable: no object — *the bees died off*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To die one after another until few or none are left.
examples: The bees *died off* over the winter.
Whole orchards *die off* in a drought like this.
The last speakers of the dialect have been *dying off* for decades.
contrast: *Die off* is one by one until the group shrinks; *die out* is the end of the whole kind: *the species died out*.

separable: no object — *the custom died out*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To disappear completely over time, leaving nothing of its kind.
examples: That custom *died out* fifty years ago.
Languages *die out* when children stop speaking them.
The breed had nearly *died out* by 1900.
contrast: Spelling trap: *die* → *dying*, never ✗ *dieing*.

separable: inseparable — *dip into savings*, *dip into it*; never ✗ *dip savings into*.
gloss: To spend part of money you had been keeping for something else.
examples: We had to *dip into* savings to fix the roof.
He *dips into* his bonus every December.
They have been *dipping into* the emergency fund all year.
contrast: Doubled consonant: *dip* → *dipped*, *dipping*.

separable: inseparable — *dip into a book*, *dip into it*; never ✗ *dip a book into*.
gloss: To read or look at small parts of something rather than all of it.
examples: I *dip into* the cookbook whenever I need an idea.
She *dipped into* the memoir on the plane and put it down.
He has only *dipped into* the report so far.

separable: separable — *dish out advice* / *dish advice out*, and with a pronoun it must split: *dish it out*.
gloss: To hand something out freely, especially criticism, advice, or punishment.
examples: He *dishes out* advice nobody asked for.
The referee *dished out* four penalties in ten minutes.
He can *dish it out*, but he cannot take it.
contrast: The fixed line *dish it out* (and cannot take it) is the form learners hear most.

separable: separable — *dish up the pasta* / *dish the pasta up*, and *dish it up*.
transitivity: both — transitive (dish up the stew), intransitive (I will dish up while the bread is warm)
gloss: To serve food onto plates, or to serve up something ready-made.
examples: Grandma *dished up* three plates before anyone sat down.
I will *dish up* while the bread is still warm.
They are *dishing up* the same excuses as last year.

ru: обходиться, обойтись без; отказываться, отказаться от
separable: inseparable — *dispense with the formalities*, *dispense with them*; never ✗ *dispense them with*.
gloss: To stop using or doing something because it is not necessary.
examples: Let us *dispense with* the introductions and get to work.
The judge *dispensed with* the usual formalities.
They have *dispensed with* paper tickets entirely.
contrast: Slightly formal. In everyday speech Americans say *do without* or *skip*.

ru: приниматься, приняться (с ходу); бросаться, броситься (в дело)
separable: no object — *just dive in*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To start doing something eagerly and without hesitating.
examples: Do not overthink it — just *dive in*.
She *dived in* on her first day and cleared the backlog.
They are *diving in* without a plan, as usual.
contrast: Americans say both *dived in* and *dove in* for the past; the participle is only *dived in*: *has dived in*.

ru: погружаться, погрузиться (с головой во что-л.); браться, взяться (за что-л.)
separable: inseparable — *dive into the numbers*, *dive into them*; never ✗ *dive the numbers into*.
gloss: To begin working on or examining something with great energy.
examples: Let us *dive into* the numbers before lunch.
He *dived into* the project and forgot to eat.
We have been *diving into* the archives all week.
contrast: Past tense: *dived into* and *dove into* are both American; only *dived into* works as the participle.

separable: separable — *divide up the chores* / *divide the chores up*, and *divide them up*.
gloss: To separate something into parts and share them out.
examples: We *divided up* the chores by floor.
*Divide* the class *up* into four groups.
The land has been *divided up* among the heirs.

separable: separable — *divvy up the tips* / *divvy the tips up*, and *divvy them up*.
gloss: To share something out in portions among a group, informally.
examples: They *divvied up* the tips at closing.
Let us *divvy* the check *up* evenly.
The leftovers were *divvied up* before I got there.
contrast: Informal but very common in American speech. Spelling: *divvies*, *divvied*, yet *divvying* keeps the *y*.

separable: separable, and nearly always reflexive or passive — *doll herself up*, *get dolled up*, *all dolled up*.
gloss: To dress someone, usually yourself, in showy, festive clothes.
examples: She *dolls* herself *up* for every family photo.
They got *dolled up* for prom.
The whole cast was *dolled up* in forties clothes.
contrast: Informal and a little old-fashioned; the living form is the passive *all dolled up*.

separable: separable — *dole out the candy* / *dole the candy out*, and *dole it out*.
gloss: To give something out in small amounts, a little at a time.
examples: The office *doles out* parking passes one per floor.
He *doled* the candy *out* piece by piece.
Praise was *doled out* sparingly in that house.

separable: inseparable — *dote on the baby*, *dote on her*; never ✗ *dote her on*.
gloss: To show someone a great deal of affection, often more than is good for them.
examples: He *dotes on* his granddaughter.
They *doted on* that dog for fifteen years.
She has always *doted on* her youngest.

ru: возвращаться, вернуться тем же путём; поворачивать, повернуть назад
separable: no object — *we doubled back*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To turn around and go back the way you came.
examples: We *doubled back* when the trail flooded.
The road *doubles back* on itself twice.
He was *doubling back* to look for his keys.

ru: идти, пойти на обострение; удваивать, удвоить ставку (на что-л.)
separable: no object — what you commit to follows *on*: *double down on the plan*. Nothing sits between the two words.
gloss: To commit even harder to a course of action, especially a risky one, instead of backing off.
examples: Instead of apologizing, he *doubled down*.
The company is *doubling down* on electric models.
They have *doubled down* on a strategy that clearly is not working.
contrast: From blackjack, where you double the bet. Today it is mostly about opinions and strategy, not money.

separable: usually no object — *he doubled over*. When it does take one, the object splits the two words: *the punch doubled him over*.
transitivity: both — intransitive (he doubled over), transitive (the punch doubled him over)
gloss: To bend forward sharply at the waist, from pain or laughter.
examples: He *doubled over* laughing at his own joke.
A cramp like that makes you *double over* fast.
They were *doubled over* with laughter by the end of it.

ru: селиться, поселиться вдвоём; делить, разделить (комнату, смену) с кем-л.
separable: no object in this sense — *double up in one room*, *double up on rooms*; nothing sits between the two words.
gloss: To share a room, a bed, or a shift with someone because there is not enough to go around.
examples: The boys will *double up* in the back bedroom.
We *doubled up* on hotel rooms to save money.
Two nurses have been *doubling up* on nights all month.

separable: no object — *he dozed off*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To fall lightly asleep, usually without meaning to.
examples: He *dozes off* in front of the TV every night.
I *dozed off* for maybe ten minutes.
She was *dozing off* by the second act.

separable: separable — *drag down the average* / *drag the average down*, and with a pronoun it must split: *drag you down*.
gloss: To make someone or something weaker, worse, or less successful.
examples: One bad quarter *dragged down* the whole year.
Do not let him *drag* you *down* with him.
Low turnout has been *dragging down* the numbers since March.
contrast: Doubled consonant: *drag* → *dragged*, *dragging*, never ✗ *draged*.

separable: the person always sits between the two parts — *drag me into this*, never ✗ *drag into me this*.
gloss: To involve someone in a situation they want no part of.
examples: Do not *drag* me *into* your argument with your brother.
She was *dragged into* a lawsuit over a fence.
He keeps *dragging* the kids *into* it.

separable: no object — *the meeting dragged on*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To continue for far longer than it should.
examples: The meeting *dragged on* for three hours.
Negotiations *drag on* every spring.
The trial has been *dragging on* since March.

separable: separable — *drag out the goodbyes* / *drag the goodbyes out*, and *drag it out*.
gloss: To make something last much longer than it needs to.
examples: They *dragged out* the goodbyes for an hour.
Do not *drag* it *out* — just tell her.
The case is being *dragged out* on purpose.

separable: separable — *drag up the past* / *drag the past up*, and *drag it up*.
gloss: To mention something from the past that other people would rather forget.
examples: Why *drag up* what happened in 2009?
He *dragged* my old job *up* in front of everyone.
She keeps *dragging up* the same argument.

separable: separable — *dredge up an old scandal* / *dredge an old scandal up*, and *dredge it up*.
gloss: To bring back a forgotten memory or old story, usually an unpleasant one.
examples: The article *dredged up* a scandal from the eighties.
Therapy *dredges up* things you thought were buried.
He has *dredged up* every mistake she ever made.
contrast: *Dredge up* digs out something long buried; *drag up* is closer to simply raising a sore subject again.

separable: separable — *dress down the whole crew* / *dress the whole crew down*, and with a pronoun it must split: *dress him down*.
gloss: To scold someone severely, often in front of other people.
examples: The coach *dressed* him *down* in front of the whole team.
She *dresses down* anyone who shows up late.
He was *dressed down* by his own lawyer.
contrast: The noun is written as one word: *he got a dressing-down*.

separable: no object — *everyone dresses down on Fridays*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To wear clothes that are more casual than the occasion usually calls for.
examples: Everyone *dresses down* on Fridays.
He *dressed down* for the interview and regretted it.
They have been *dressing down* since the office went hybrid.

separable: no object in this sense, or a reflexive one — *dress up for dinner*, *dress yourself up*.
gloss: To put on nicer clothes than you usually wear.
examples: You do not have to *dress up* — it is just pizza.
She *dressed up* for her first day at the firm.
We were all *dressed up* with nowhere to go.

separable: separable when it takes an object — *dress up the kids* / *dress the kids up*, *dress them up*; with no object, *dress up as a pirate*.
transitivity: both — intransitive (dress up as a pirate), transitive (dress the kids up)
gloss: To put on a costume so as to look like someone or something else.
examples: The kids *dress up* as superheroes every October.
He *dressed up* as Lincoln for the school assembly.
They are *dressing* the dog *up* again.

ru: приукрашивать, приукрасить; подавать в выгодном свете
separable: separable — *dress up the numbers* / *dress the numbers up*, and *dress it up*.
gloss: To make something look or sound better than it really is.
examples: You cannot *dress up* a bad quarter with nice charts.
He *dressed* the résumé *up* with invented titles.
The proposal has been *dressed up* as a compromise.

ru: отдаляться, отдалиться (друг от друга); расходиться, разойтись
separable: no object — *we drifted apart*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To slowly become less close to someone until the friendship fades.
examples: We *drifted apart* after college.
Couples *drift apart* when nobody is paying attention.
They had been *drifting apart* for years before the divorce.

separable: no object — *I drifted off*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To fall asleep gradually.
examples: I *drifted off* during the second half.
He *drifts off* the minute the car starts moving.
She was *drifting off* when the phone rang.
contrast: *Drift off*, *doze off* and *drop off* all mean falling asleep. *Drift off* is the gentlest and the most common in writing.

separable: no object — the topic follows *about*: *drone on about taxes*. Nothing sits between the two words.
gloss: To talk in a dull, flat voice for far too long.
examples: He *droned on* about parking for twenty minutes.
She *drones on* whenever that topic comes up.
The speaker was still *droning on* when we left.

separable: nothing can come between the two words. A place may follow straight after — *drop by the office* — but never ✗ *drop the office by*.
transitivity: both — intransitive (drop by tonight), transitive (drop by the office)
gloss: To visit briefly, usually without arranging it first.
examples: *Drop by* any time after six.
She *dropped by* with soup on Sunday.
I have been *dropping by* the shop on my way home.
contrast: Doubled consonant: *drop* → *dropped*, *dropping*.

separable: no object — the person visited follows *on*: *drop in on your aunt*, never ✗ *drop her in*.
gloss: To visit someone briefly and without warning.
examples: Feel free to *drop in* on your way through town.
My neighbor *dropped in* twice yesterday.
They are *dropping in* on us this weekend.
contrast: *Drop in* takes *on* before a person (*drop in on Sue*); *drop by* takes the place directly (*drop by Sue's*).

ru: подвозить, подвезти; завозить, завезти; высаживать, высадить
separable: separable — *drop off the kids* / *drop the kids off*, and with a pronoun it must split: *drop them off*.
gloss: To take someone or something to a place and leave them there.
examples: I will *drop off* the package on my way downtown.
She *drops* the kids *off* at seven every morning.
He was *dropped off* at the wrong terminal.
contrast: Doubled consonant: *drop* → *dropped*, *dropping*.

separable: no object — *he dropped off*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To fall asleep, especially without intending to.
examples: He *dropped off* before the movie ended.
The baby *drops off* faster in the car.
I was *dropping off* when the alarm went.

separable: no object — *sales dropped off*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To become less in number or amount.
examples: Sales *dropped off* right after the holidays.
Attendance *drops off* every August.
Donations have been *dropping off* since the spring.

separable: no object — what you leave follows *of*: *drop out of school*, never ✗ *drop school out*.
gloss: To leave a school, course, or contest before finishing it.
examples: He *dropped out* in his junior year.
Two runners *drop out* every mile in heat like this.
She has *dropped out* of the program twice now.
contrast: The noun is one word: *a college dropout*.

separable: separable — *drown out the announcement* / *drown the announcement out*, and with a pronoun it must split: *drown him out*.
gloss: To be so loud that another sound cannot be heard.
examples: The band *drowned out* the announcement.
Traffic *drowns* him *out* on that corner.
Her voice was *drowned out* by the crowd.

separable: separable — *drum up business* / *drum business up*, and *drum it up*.
gloss: To get support, business, or interest by working at it.
examples: They are *drumming up* business with free samples.
He *drummed up* enough votes to win the seat.
Support has been *drummed up* mostly online.
contrast: Doubled consonant: *drum* → *drummed*, *drumming*.

separable: separable when it takes an object — *dry off the dog* / *dry the dog off*, *dry him off*; with no object, *dry off first*.
transitivity: both — transitive (dry the dog off), intransitive (dry off before you come in)
gloss: To remove the water from the surface of something, or to get dry that way.
examples: *Dry off* before you come inside.
She *dried* the dog *off* in the garage.
The kids are *drying off* on the porch.
contrast: The *-y* changes: *dries*, *dried*, but *drying* keeps it.

separable: separable when it takes an object — *dry out the boots* / *dry the boots out*, *dry them out*; with no object, *the soil dried out*.
transitivity: both — transitive (dry out the boots), intransitive (the soil dries out)
gloss: To lose all its moisture, or to make something lose it.
examples: The soil *dries out* fast in August.
My hands *dried out* from all the soap.
We have been *drying out* the boots by the stove.
contrast: *Dry out* is about moisture leaving the inside of a thing; *dry off* is only the wet surface.

ru: проходить, пройти курс от алкоголизма; завязывать, завязать с выпивкой
separable: no object — *he is drying out*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To stop drinking alcohol long enough to become sober, usually in a clinic.
examples: He spent a month upstate *drying out*.
She *dried out* at a clinic in Arizona.
The doctor told him he cannot *dry out* on his own.
contrast: Informal. Related to the adjective *dry* meaning sober: *he has been dry for six years*.

separable: usually no object — *the creek dried up*. With an object it separates: *the sun dried up the puddles* / *dried them up*.
transitivity: both — intransitive (the creek dried up), transitive (the sun dried up the puddles)
gloss: To lose all its water and become completely dry.
examples: The creek *dries up* every July.
The puddles *dried up* by noon.
The well has *dried up* twice this decade.

ru: иссякать, иссякнуть; прекращаться, прекратиться (о потоке денег, заказов)
separable: no object — a supply *dries up* on its own; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: Of a supply of money, work, or interest: to stop coming altogether.
examples: Funding *dried up* after the first year.
Offers *dry up* fast once the season ends.
Their donations have been *drying up* since the scandal.

separable: no object — *he ducked out*; nothing can come between the two words.
gloss: To leave a place quickly and quietly, hoping nobody notices.
examples: He *ducked out* before the speeches started.
I am going to *duck out* early today.
She has been *ducking out* at lunch to make calls.

separable: inseparable — *duck out of jury duty*, *duck out of it*; never ✗ *duck jury duty out of*.
gloss: To avoid a duty or a commitment you had agreed to.
examples: You cannot *duck out of* jury duty that easily.
He *ducked out of* the family photo again.
They are always *ducking out of* cleanup.

ru: упрощать, упростить (в ущерб содержанию); опошлять, опошлить
separable: separable — *dumb down the material* / *dumb the material down*, and *dumb it down*.
gloss: To make something simpler in a way that throws away what mattered.
examples: Do not *dumb down* the explanation for them.
They *dumbed* the whole curriculum *down*.
The textbook has been *dumbed down* for the new edition.
contrast: Always critical — to *dumb something down* is never a compliment. The *b* in *dumb* stays silent in every form.

ru: набрасываться, наброситься (с критикой); сваливать, свалить (проблемы на кого-л.)
separable: inseparable — *dump on the mayor*, *dump on me*; never ✗ *dump me on*. A different pattern takes an object first: *dump your problems on me*.
gloss: To criticize someone harshly, or to unload your troubles onto them.
examples: The press *dumped on* the mayor all week.
Sorry for *dumping on* you — it has been a long day.
He *dumps on* whoever answers the phone.
contrast: Informal and American. In Britain the criticism sense is usually *have a go at someone*.

separable: separable — *dust off the old résumé* / *dust the old résumé off*, and *dust it off*.
gloss: To bring something back into use after a long time unused.
examples: He *dusted off* his old résumé on Sunday night.
She *dusts* that recipe *off* every Thanksgiving.
They have *dusted off* a play from the eighties.

ru: зацикливаться, зациклиться на; долго останавливаться, остановиться на
separable: inseparable — *dwell on the mistake*, *dwell on it*; never ✗ *dwell it on*.
gloss: To keep thinking or talking about something unpleasant for too long.
examples: Try not to *dwell on* it tonight.
He *dwelled on* that one mistake for months.
She has been *dwelling on* the diagnosis since Friday.
contrast: Americans write *dwelled*; British English prefers *dwelt*. Both are understood.
